rk_fulltext_followup.reading: All37 pages read as extracted text or rendered page6, including all47references. Rendered pages6,8,15,17 inspected. Remaining figures/tables and many proof displays are not yet visually checked; no general proof or implementation certification.
observations: Definition1 p6 defines vertex diameter as maximum vertex count among shortest paths; on unit-weight graphs it is edge diameter plus one. This resolves the minimum-versus-maximum wording ambiguity in the later KADABRA text.
Theorem1 p8 uses a universal positive constant c; the following sentence describes approximately.5 as an estimate. This is not an inspected proof that c=.5 is sufficient universally.

Equation3 p15 includes floor(log2(VD-2))+1+ln(1/delta), but Algorithm1 line5 p17 omits +1. Any transcription must preserve the discrepancy and use a justified bound. Integer rounding and VD<=2 remain explicit boundary conditions.

Section5.1 pp15-16 samples all ordered distinct pairs, then a shortest path uniformly. Unreachable pairs correspond to the empty path and do not update node scores. Backtracking weights predecessors by path counts.

Section5.1 pp17-18 discusses an undirected equal-weight diameter upper bound and largest weakly connected component size for directed/unequal-weight graphs. No all-scope implementation, general VC proof or benchmark assessment is complete.
rk_fulltext_followup.next_check: Inspect remaining source diagrams, resolve core versus variant domains, deduplicate native candidates and mappings, and construct finite path-law/cap checks. The all-node RK procedure, relative top-k, edge, bounded-distance and walk variants remain separate assessment candidates.

observations: The unique-shortest-path VC bound of3 is explicitly restricted to undirected graphs in Lemma2 p10; pp11-12 give a directed counterexample. Do not use the abbreviated p20 paragraph as a directed guarantee.
The m>=2 condition on p9 does not imply vertex diameter>2: a triangle has three edges and all shortest paths have two vertices. Small-diameter cases need separate handling before using log(VD-2).

The top-K procedure uses ell-prime=bhat-K-epsilon; it can be nonpositive. Algorithm2 p21 uses delta-double-prime in its first-phase line, whereas prose p20 uses delta-prime. The theorem and output-set scope require further checking before curation.

Lemma8 point3 p21 appears overbroad: excluding all non-top-K vertices with estimates above ell-prime(1+epsilon) does not follow merely from a relative approximation above ell-prime. This remains an unresolved source claim, not an adopted guarantee.

The path-domain union collapses a shared empty path unless endpoint identities or aggregate empty-path mass are retained. Pair-then-path sampling itself has unambiguous zero contributions for unreachable pairs; do not substitute an improperly normalized path distribution.

The equal-sample-count BP variance comparison is for iid source sampling under the paper’s normalized estimator. It is not a universal runtime superiority result or a guarantee for nonuniform/deterministic pivots.

additional_scope_limits: Section6.1 p25 alternates path-size thresholds k+1 and k; Section6.2 p26 alternates internal-node ranges and updates to all touched vertices. These variants need original-source and visual assessment before adopting precise estimands.

The experimental implementation is C with igraph and Python3.3.1, on AMD PhenomIIX4 955/16GB/Debianwheezy Linux3.2.0. It uses c=.5,delta.1 and five runs. Figures include six undirected and six directed networks plus generated Barabasi-Albert scaling cases; no quantitative speedup or general confidence validation is adopted.
The experimental prose calls n-2 a diameter upper bound and labels soc-Epinions1 inconsistently. Definition1 gives vertex diameter up to n; no numeric benchmark convention is silently repaired.
No source references beyond the cited primary manuscripts were fully inspected merely because they appear in this reference list. No author software or model training was executed.

entries.name: KADABRA balanced bidirectional shortest-path sampling
entries.definition: A shortest-path sampling algorithm that expands complete breadth-first-search frontiers from opposite endpoints according to frontier edge volume, then samples a connecting edge and its two path segments with shortest-path-count weights to obtain a uniform shortest path.

claims.statement: For a finite simple unweighted directed or undirected graph and distinct specified endpoints s and t, the output is a uniformly sampled shortest s-to-t path when one exists, and an empty result otherwise. This conditional sampler does not itself select the endpoint distribution or estimate centrality. KADABRA’s enclosing estimator uses independent uniform ordered distinct-node pairs, which is an additional sampling layer.

evidence.locator: Sections 2 and 4, PDF pp. 4–7; Appendix A notation, p. 15

claims.statement: Maintain source and target BFS layers, distances and exact shortest-path counts. At each step expand the entire current frontier with smaller incident-edge volume, breaking equal-volume ties by a fixed convention. In directed graphs the source search uses outgoing arcs and the target search uses incoming arcs. Collect all connecting edges encountered in the selected frontier before choosing a path. The balance criterion is edge volume, not merely the number of frontier vertices or the total sizes of the two search trees.

evidence.locator: Section 4, PDF p. 7; explicit finite implementation interpretation in research/discovery/kadabra-path-boundaries.py

claims.statement: For a source-side meeting edge (v,w), assign weight sigma_sv times sigma_wt. Sample one meeting edge in proportion to this weight, then sample a shortest prefix from s to v and shortest suffix from w to t using path-count-proportional predecessor or successor choices. Their concatenation with the edge is a shortest s-to-t path. The product of cut-edge probability and prefix/suffix probabilities gives each complete shortest path probability 1/sigma_st. Reaching a vertex a second time at the same BFS distance must still contribute to its path count.

evidence.locator: Section 4, PDF p. 7; path-count factorization checked in research/discovery/kadabra-path-boundaries.py. The probability product and equal-distance accumulation are explicit curator interpretation of the source’s counting requirement.

claims.statement: Exact curator enumeration checks every ordered distinct-endpoint pair in all 64 undirected and 4096 directed simple four-node graphs, including disconnected cases. A separate directed branching example has meeting-edge weights 2 and 1, giving three complete paths probability 1/3 each; uniform meeting-edge selection would instead give probabilities 1/4, 1/4 and 1/2. These finite cases illustrate why full-frontier processing and exact counts matter; they do not certify author software or all possible graph implementations.

evidence.locator: Section 4, PDF p. 7; finite exhaustive and branching calculations in research/discovery/kadabra-path-boundaries.py

claims.statement: The sampler retains linear worst-case graph-traversal work; a selected 129-node path requires scanning 254 incident edges in the curator calculation. The source’s sublinear analyses concern specified configuration and rank-one inhomogeneous random-graph models with additional degree-distribution and supercriticality assumptions, not every graph or endpoint pair under every model. Its unit-cost arithmetic assumption also hides the bit cost of potentially exponential shortest-path counts. Weighted edges, approximate counts and a universal square-root runtime are outside this maintained scope.

evidence.locator: Section 4 and Theorem 4, PDF pp. 7–8; Appendix E, pp. 20–24; long-path calculation in research/discovery/kadabra-path-boundaries.py

claims.statement: The sampler is a subroutine distinct from KADABRA’s confidence budgets, bounded adaptive stopping and top-k output. Replacing an exact pair contribution by one sampled path indicator changes the estimator variance even when the mean target is unchanged. The 2016 historical experiments describe the sampler within a particular implementation and graph collection; they are not a general performance guarantee. Other balancing or parallelization variants are outside this record’s scope.

evidence.locator: Abstract and Sections 2, 4 and 6, PDF pp. 1, 4–8 and 9–12; finite indicator-versus-fraction comparison in research/discovery/kadabra-path-boundaries.py. Other algorithms are not included in this maintained identity.

examined_targets.rejection_reason: Sampling a path does not group vertices into clusters.
Uniformly sampling a conditional shortest path does not group vertices into clusters, whether or not labels are available.
The identity is a randomized graph-search and path-sampling procedure, not merely an input-output function.
The defined output is a sampled shortest path; incidental downstream feature use does not establish a data-preparation identity.
The conditional graph-path sampler has no language-model objective, training mechanism or learned representation.
A sampled graph path is not a belief about the relevance of highly ranked information.
A specified uniform conditional path law is an algorithm, not a selection-bias concept.
A graph-path sampling procedure is not subgroup representation bias.
Neither labels nor a deep neural network are acquired or fitted.
Conditional shortest-path sampling does not itself define a data-dredging bias.
This AIO class wraps recurrent neural networks; forward and reverse graph searches do not instantiate that layer.

limitations: Exact simple unweighted graph paths and exact counts are assumed. Weighted shortest paths, multiedge conventions, finite-precision sampling and approximate count correction require separate analysis.
The conditional endpoint sampler does not by itself define a centrality estimator or its accuracy, confidence, stopping rule or endpoint population.
Uniformity requires processing the full chosen frontier and count-weighted meeting-edge and segment choices. A generic bidirectional search that returns its first meeting path is not equivalent.

Finite exact calculations and source interpretation are curator checks, not execution or verification of the authors’ implementation. Some random-graph proof displays were read only as extracted text.
No universal runtime improvement, current-software comparison or proof of every reported random-graph bound is asserted. DRAFT remains after author self-review.

primary_analysis.mechanism: Static unweighted directed/undirected graph; iid uniform ordered distinct pairs and uniform shortest paths, with unreachable pairs empty and internal-node indicators. Balanced bidirectional BFS expands complete lower-edge-volume frontiers and samples meeting edges proportional to prefix/suffix path counts; it must finish the frontier before selecting. The stopped-sampling procedure has a deterministic positive integer horizon and node failure budgets fixed before the main iid stream.
primary_analysis.pilot: AppendixD pp19-20 takes alpha=omega/100 pilot paths before starting the algorithm. Algorithm1 resets counts afterward. Budgets selected using an independent pilot can be conditioned upon for the main-run argument. Source sets positive floors; zero pilot coefficients and an all-zero pilot need explicit handling before implementing the heuristic.
source_cautions: Algorithm1 p6 uses raw counters where confidence formulas need means, starts at tau=0 and prints tau increment beside the per-node update. A faithful mathematical description must use positive-time means and increment once per sampled path, including empty paths; no literal pseudocode implementation is certified.

The source horizon expression needs integer rounding and has a log(VD-2) boundary. Its RK constant/diameter inputs require primary verification. An independently justified fixed-time cap may be specified as an explicit curator alternative, not silently substituted.

At true and estimated centrality zero, f=0; the inclusive lower-tail event in Theorem9 p17 then occurs with probability1. Use closed-interval coverage with strict outside errors and preserve the printed equality issue. AppendixC p18 repeats E1 in the union bound and reverses a displayed E2 upper-tail inequality.

AppendixB p16 omits the factor2 in a two-sided Hoeffding display; its following remark includes it. Theorem8 p17 has conditional-variance/index/square notation issues. Do not copy these as certified general theorems.

Algorithm2 p16 uses epsilon=.0001 whereas AppendixD p20 says.001, returns b despite its budget output specification, and the prose calls for a largest C although the exponential sum decreases with C. The printed formulas and optimization need separate transcription checks.
Algorithm3 uses boundary adjacent-rank indices. Top-k output may exceed k and contain uncertain ranks; neither exact unique ordering nor causal importance follows.

Random-graph speedup is conditional on configuration/rank-one models, degree convergence/moments, supercriticality and O(1) path-count arithmetic. Remaining proof displays are not all visually checked and no general or worst-case square-root runtime is adopted.

Figure2 caption uses n as exponent base while main text defines log(m_avg)/log(m). Tables include slower KADABRA cases; p27 subelj-jung-j-jung-j at lambda.005 reports.216s versus ABRA-1.2 .211s, and p28 lambda.020 reports.217s versus RK.176s and ABRA-1.2 .045s. These are source examples, not replicated measurements.

conference_reading.mechanism: For static unweighted directed/undirected graphs, sample uniform distinct endpoint pairs and uniform shortest paths; internal-node indicators estimate the n(n-1)-normalized score. The confidence procedure uses a deterministic maximum sample horizon and fixed node-specific lower/upper failure budgets; stopped-martingale inequalities, rather than a fixed-time bound substituted at an arbitrary stopping time, justify adaptive stopping.

rk_fulltext_followup.reading: All37 pages read as extracted text or rendered page6, including all47references. Rendered pages6,8,15,17 inspected. Remaining figures/tables and many proof displays are not yet visually checked; no general proof or implementation certification.
observations: Definition1 p6 defines vertex diameter as maximum vertex count among shortest paths; on unit-weight graphs it is edge diameter plus one. This resolves the minimum-versus-maximum wording ambiguity in the later KADABRA text.
Theorem1 p8 uses a universal positive constant c; the following sentence describes approximately.5 as an estimate. This is not an inspected proof that c=.5 is sufficient universally.

Equation3 p15 includes floor(log2(VD-2))+1+ln(1/delta), but Algorithm1 line5 p17 omits +1. Any transcription must preserve the discrepancy and use a justified bound. Integer rounding and VD<=2 remain explicit boundary conditions.

Section5.1 pp15-16 samples all ordered distinct pairs, then a shortest path uniformly. Unreachable pairs correspond to the empty path and do not update node scores. Backtracking weights predecessors by path counts.

Section5.1 pp17-18 discusses an undirected equal-weight diameter upper bound and largest weakly connected component size for directed/unequal-weight graphs. No all-scope implementation, general VC proof or benchmark assessment is complete.
rk_fulltext_followup.next_check: Inspect remaining source diagrams, resolve core versus variant domains, deduplicate native candidates and mappings, and construct finite path-law/cap checks. The all-node RK procedure, relative top-k, edge, bounded-distance and walk variants remain separate assessment candidates.

observations: The unique-shortest-path VC bound of3 is explicitly restricted to undirected graphs in Lemma2 p10; pp11-12 give a directed counterexample. Do not use the abbreviated p20 paragraph as a directed guarantee.
The m>=2 condition on p9 does not imply vertex diameter>2: a triangle has three edges and all shortest paths have two vertices. Small-diameter cases need separate handling before using log(VD-2).

The top-K procedure uses ell-prime=bhat-K-epsilon; it can be nonpositive. Algorithm2 p21 uses delta-double-prime in its first-phase line, whereas prose p20 uses delta-prime. The theorem and output-set scope require further checking before curation.

Lemma8 point3 p21 appears overbroad: excluding all non-top-K vertices with estimates above ell-prime(1+epsilon) does not follow merely from a relative approximation above ell-prime. This remains an unresolved source claim, not an adopted guarantee.

The path-domain union collapses a shared empty path unless endpoint identities or aggregate empty-path mass are retained. Pair-then-path sampling itself has unambiguous zero contributions for unreachable pairs; do not substitute an improperly normalized path distribution.

The equal-sample-count BP variance comparison is for iid source sampling under the paper’s normalized estimator. It is not a universal runtime superiority result or a guarantee for nonuniform/deterministic pivots.

additional_scope_limits: Section6.1 p25 alternates path-size thresholds k+1 and k; Section6.2 p26 alternates internal-node ranges and updates to all touched vertices. These variants need original-source and visual assessment before adopting precise estimands.

The experimental implementation is C with igraph and Python3.3.1, on AMD PhenomIIX4 955/16GB/Debianwheezy Linux3.2.0. It uses c=.5,delta.1 and five runs. Figures include six undirected and six directed networks plus generated Barabasi-Albert scaling cases; no quantitative speedup or general confidence validation is adopted.
The experimental prose calls n-2 a diameter upper bound and labels soc-Epinions1 inconsistently. Definition1 gives vertex diameter up to n; no numeric benchmark convention is silently repaired.

native_neighbors.name: ABRA-s-fix fixed-sample betweenness approximation
native_neighbors.definition: A fixed-sample static-graph betweenness algorithm that averages shortest-path fractions over a user-specified number of uniform endpoint pairs and returns both the estimates and a simultaneous Rademacher-based additive error bound, regardless of the size of that bound.

native_neighbors.name: ABRA-s progressive betweenness approximation
native_neighbors.definition: A progressive sampling algorithm for static-graph betweenness that averages fractions of shortest paths through each node over uniformly sampled endpoint pairs and checks a predetermined sequence of sample sizes and stops when a Rademacher-based simultaneous error bound meets the requested additive tolerance.

native_neighbors.name: AND/OR abstraction sampling
native_neighbors.definition: An importance-sampling algorithm for partition functions of discrete graphical models that samples representatives in a pseudo-tree-guided AND/OR search space, allowing abstractions across branching-ancestor contexts through interleaved ancestor pruning and relative-weight value backup.

native_neighbors.name: A-star search
native_neighbors.definition: A heuristic graph-search method that selects an open node using the sum of its best known path cost from the start and an estimated remaining cost to a goal.

native_neighbors.name: Accelerated graph degree linkage
native_neighbors.definition: An approximate graph degree linkage algorithm that selects merges from maintained cluster-neighbor sets and updates those sets locally instead of searching every current cluster pair.

native_neighbors.name: Activation-Value Gaussian Pooling
native_neighbors.definition: A parameterized neural pooling unit that averages a group of transformed activations using normalized Gaussian-kernel weights determined by each activation’s distance from a learned pool mean.

native_neighbors.name: AdaMixUp
native_neighbors.definition: An adaptive interpolation-training procedure that learns example-dependent mixing-coefficient regions with a policy network and trains a classifier together with an intrusion discriminator intended to separate mixed examples from original data.

native_neighbors.name: Adafactor
native_neighbors.definition: An adaptive gradient optimization method that approximates matrix-valued second-moment statistics using row and column factors.

native_neighbors.name: Adagrad
native_neighbors.definition: An adaptive gradient optimization method that scales each coordinate's update using accumulated squared gradients.

native_neighbors.name: Adam
native_neighbors.definition: Stochastic gradient optimization using bias-corrected exponential estimates of first and second gradient moments to scale parameter updates.

native_neighbors.name: Adaptive Deconvolutional Network
native_neighbors.definition: An unsupervised hierarchical image-representation architecture that alternates convolutional sparse synthesis with spatial and cross-map pooling switches and fits each layer through a reconstruction path to the original image.

native_neighbors.name: Adaptive Metropolis
native_neighbors.definition: A history-adaptive random-walk Metropolis sampler whose Gaussian proposal covariance is estimated from the accumulated retained states, including repetitions after rejected proposals.

native_neighbors.name: Adaptive parallel tempering
native_neighbors.definition: A parallel-tempering algorithm that adapts temperature gaps and within-replica random-walk proposal parameters through projected stochastic approximation.

native_neighbors.name: Adaptive rejection sampling
native_neighbors.definition: The Gilks–Wild univariate rejection sampler that uses tangents to a concave log density as a piecewise-linear upper hull and chords as a lower hull, updating these bounds from evaluated proposals.

native_neighbors.name: Adaptive scaling Metropolis
native_neighbors.definition: A random-walk Metropolis algorithm that adapts its proposal scale through stochastic approximation driven by the proposal acceptance probability relative to a chosen target rate.

native_neighbors.name: Adaptive scaling within adaptive Metropolis
native_neighbors.definition: An adaptive Metropolis algorithm that combines acceptance-rate-driven scalar proposal scaling with recursive mean and covariance-shape adaptation from retained samples.

native_neighbors.name: Admixture of Poisson Markov random fields

native_neighbors.name: Alternating Expectation Conditional Maximization
native_neighbors.definition: A likelihood-optimization framework that alternates cycles of expectation and constrained maximization, permitting the admissible data augmentation and constraint functions to change between cycles while collectively covering the parameter directions.

native_neighbors.name: Alternating Kullback-Leibler Minimization

native_neighbors.name: Analytic moment-based Gaussian-process filtering

native_neighbors.name: Ancestral Gumbel-Top-k sampling

native_neighbors.name: Mean-field Boltzmann learning
